sources.title: Leike et al. 2018, Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling: a research direction
claims: Frames the agent alignment problem as: how can we create agents that behave in accordance with the user's intentions (intent-alignment definition; authors at DeepMind)

sources.title: Askell et al. 2021, A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment
claims: Defines an aligned AI as helpful, honest and harmless (HHH); criteria are simple and memorable but subtle, ambiguous and may conflict
What counts as harmful varies by people and culture; deployers take responsibility for how alignment is defined
Alignment techniques do not depend on a specific choice of values and could be used to train systems that do bad things

sources.title: Ouyang et al. 2022, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)
claims: States the definition of alignment has been vague and confusing with competing proposals; adopts Leike et al. intent plus a helpful/honest/harmless framework
Operationalises helpful via labeler preference ratings, honest via truthfulness (closed-domain hallucination, TruthfulQA, 'only a small part'), harmless via proxy criteria and toxicity/bias datasets
Training labelers agree with each other 72.6 +/- 1.5% on comparisons; labelers mostly English speakers in the US or Southeast Asia
Aligns to labelers, researchers and API customers; does not claim they are the right source of preferences; impossible to align to everyone at once
On its prompt distribution, human evaluators prefer 1.3B InstructGPT outputs over 175B GPT-3; models are neither fully aligned nor fully safe

sources.title: Bai et al. 2022, Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
claims: Two stages: critique-and-revision with supervised fine-tuning, then AI comparison labels, preference model and RL (RLAIF)
Only human oversight for harmlessness is a list of principles; helpfulness still uses human labels
Authors call the principles ad hoc, chosen for research, to be refined by a larger set of stakeholders

sources.title: Gabriel 2020, Artificial Intelligence, Values, and Alignment (Minds and Machines)
claims: Distinguishes alignment with instructions, intentions, revealed preferences, informed preferences, interests and values
Argues the central challenge is fair principles that receive reflective endorsement despite moral disagreement, not identifying true moral principles

sources.title: Hadfield-Menell et al. 2016, Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs + pdf, HTTP 200, 2026-10-03); abstract-level claims only
claims: Proposes a formal definition of the value alignment problem as a cooperative game where the robot does not initially know the human's reward function (authors at UC Berkeley)

sources.title: Krakovna et al. 2020, Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity (Google DeepMind blog, dated 2020-04-21)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL, HTTP 200; the old /discover/blog/ URL redirects here)
claims: Specification gaming satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome
Lego stacking example: reward on the height of the red block's bottom face, agent flips the block instead of stacking it (original study Popov et al. 2017, relayed by the post)

sources.title: Sharma et al. 2023, Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs, HTTP 200); abstract only, full treatment belongs to ai-term-sycophancy
claims: In existing human preference data, responses matching a user's views are more likely to be preferred; sycophancy likely driven in part by preference judgments

sources.title: NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails Library Developer Guide, Overview
claims: Input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output rails run at different stages of an LLM interaction
Guardrails can be added before and after LLM calls without changing the application LLM

sources.title: Anthropic Usage Policy (page states effective September 15, 2025)
claims: Applies to anyone who can submit inputs to the products; enforced with detection and monitoring
Violations can lead to throttling, suspension or termination; outputs may be blocked or modified when inputs violate the policy

sources.title: OpenAI Model Spec (2026/08/18)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL of the dated page, HTTP 200). The site root is a 234-byte meta-refresh shell to this page, and this page shows a 'newer version is available' banner whose link points back to the root; WebSearch also reports 2026-08-18 as the latest. Only the Overview statements were used.
claims: Describes intended model behavior; OpenAI says it is training models to align to the Model Spec and that production models do not yet fully reflect it
The spec is complemented by usage policies and safety protocols (testing, monitoring, mitigation)

existing_overlap: ai-term-rlhf already summarises InstructGPT's RLHF pipeline and its 'whose preferences' caveat; this article reuses InstructGPT only for how alignment was operationalised (helpful/honest/harmless proxies, who is aligned to) and links to rlhf for the training mechanics. Sycophancy (ai-term-sycophancy, batch 02) and ai-term-guardrails / ai-term-red-teaming are one-sentence mentions with links. Site news pages that mention misalignment (e.g. ai-news-openai-misalignment-reports-20260917) are not linked because they are not in the assignment's links list.
notes: Count follows pack_ingest._body_length (paragraphs, rich_paragraph text including link text, list items, table cells, callout title and text); about 2410 without link text. All examples (customer-service 'resolved' button reward, fictional product page) are labelled as illustrative and unmeasured. No model names, prices, cutoffs or leaderboard scores. Title tuned from the draft because the draft phrase equated alignment with intent alone, which contradicts the article's point that definitions differ. dry-run ingest: ok, only the repo-wide warning no_summary (no published ai-term pack carries a summary block).
